title: How a Liquidity Pool Really Works
objectives: How x · y = k prices a swap, and why that rule means a pool can never run empty
Why the same $50 trade is a rounding error in one pool and a real cost in another
Work a constant-product trade by hand until the numbers stop being abstract
The one habit that stops you overpaying on thin pools

steps.title: The Shared Piggy Bank
steps.body:
On a stock exchange you wait for a seller. On Solana's AMMs there is no order book and nobody to wait for. You trade against a shared pot of tokens that anyone can fill and anyone can draw from.

Simply put, a liquidity pool is a wallet the market owns. It holds two tokens — here SOL and fUSDC — and it prices every trade off the ratio sitting between them.

The pot obeys one rule:

`x · y = k`

x is the SOL inside, y is the fUSDC inside, and k is the product of the two. A swap is not allowed to change k. You cannot empty the pot, because pushing SOL out forces y upward, which makes every remaining SOL more expensive.

Depth is what decides how much that costs you. The pool you will trade in the simulator holds about $4,000. The deep pool holds about $400,000. Same $50 order in both. One is a visible fraction of the shallow pot; the other is dust. That self-inflicted price move is <Term id="price_impact">price impact</Term>, and it is the most common way a swap quietly returns less than you expected.

steps.title: The Liquidity Lab

goal.description: Switch between the shallow and deep pools on a 50 fUSDC trade and watch price impact fall from over 2.4% to under 0.05%.

hints: Switch the pool selector to the Deep pool.
Watch the price impact readout collapse toward zero.
Then drag the trade slider up to 500 fUSDC and see how much worse the shallow pool gets.

steps.title: What Just Happened? Price Impact
steps.body:
Same 50 fUSDC, two very different fills.

In the shallow pool the trade was a meaningful slice of the vault, so the curve pushed the price several percent against you before the swap finished. That cost never shows up as a line item on the confirmation screen.

In the deep pool the same order was a rounding error. Impact dropped below 0.05% and you received measurably more SOL for the exact same input.

Price impact stacks with <Term id="slippage">slippage</Term> to decide what actually lands in your wallet. A <Term id="quote">quote</Term> you accept and a fill you receive stop being the same thing the moment a pool has to move.

The habit worth building: look at the pool's reserves before you size a trade. If your order is more than a fraction of a percent of the pool, split it, route through an aggregator, or find a deeper pool.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Deriving x · y = k
steps.body:
Let's derive the curve by hand so the number stops being abstract.

A pool holds 100 SOL and 10,000 USDC, so `k = 100 × 10,000 = 1,000,000`.

You swap 10 SOL in. The SOL reserve becomes 110. To hold k constant the USDC reserve must become `1,000,000 / 110 ≈ 9,090.91`.

You receive `10,000 − 9,090.91 ≈ 909.09 USDC`.

The spot price before your trade was $100 per SOL. Your effective price was $90.91. That 9.09% gap is price impact, and it is calculated before any <Term id="liquidity_pool">pool</Term> fee — most AMMs charge another 0.25% to 0.3% on top.

Two things to notice. Impact is not linear: a trade twice the size does not simply cost twice as much, because x sits in the denominator. And impact is always a property of your order relative to the pool's size. A 10 SOL trade into a pool holding 10,000 SOL is a completely different event.

questions.prompt: What does 'k' represent in the constant product formula x · y = k?
options: The daily transaction volume of the exchange
The invariant product of the two token reserves, which AMM smart contracts preserve across every swap
The network gas fee paid to Solana validators
The total number of users who have joined the pool
questions.explainRight: 'k' is the invariant: reserve A multiplied by reserve B. Every swap has to leave that product unchanged, which is why the pool always has a price for any trade size and can never be emptied.
questions.explainWrong: Not gas fees and not user counts. k is simply the product of the two reserves, held constant by the contract. That one constraint is what lets an <Term id="amm">AMM</Term> work without an order book.

questions.prompt: Why can't traders simply drain a pool of all its SOL in one giant buy?
options: Because as the SOL reserve shrinks, each remaining SOL becomes more expensive, so buying the last coins becomes unattractive
Because AMM pools hard-lock withdrawals after 10 trades in a day
Because Solana validators block any transaction larger than 1% of pool reserves
Because the pool automatically re-mints SOL the moment reserves get low
questions.explainRight: The last coins are the expensive ones. As SOL leaves, x shrinks and the invariant forces each remaining SOL up in price, so the trade stops being affordable long before the pot empties.
questions.explainWrong: There is no daily trade limit and no validator rule involved. The protection is arithmetic: a shrinking reserve makes each remaining unit cost dramatically more.

questions.prompt: You want to swap a large amount of tokens with the least possible price impact. What should you look for?
options: A pool with the highest fee tier
A pool created less than a minute ago
A pool with high Total Value Locked (deep liquidity)
A pool with only 1 holder
questions.explainRight: Depth is the size of the vault. A big order in a big pool is a small fraction of the reserves, so the price barely moves.
questions.explainWrong: Fee tier and pool age have nothing to do with it. What matters is reserves measured against your order size — a shallow pot turns an ordinary trade into a wave.

questions.prompt: A pool holds 100 SOL and 10,000 USDC. A trader swaps in 10 SOL. Roughly how much USDC do they receive?
questions.explainRight: You add 10 SOL, so x becomes 110. To hold k at 1,000,000 the USDC side has to fall to about 9,091, which leaves you roughly $909. Against the $100 spot price that is about a $9 haircut — your price impact.
questions.explainWrong: Do the division, not the multiplication. With x at 110 the USDC reserve must drop to around 9,091 to keep the product constant, so the payout is about $909.

questions.prompt: After you buy SOL from an AMM, why does the next SOL you buy cost slightly more?
options: The pool re-prices every hour using yesterday's trades
Buying SOL shrinks the SOL reserve, so each remaining SOL is scarcer and the curve prices it higher
The pool charges a hidden surcharge on repeat buyers
Validators impose a memory tax on frequent traders
questions.explainRight: Every buy shrinks x, and the invariant turns that scarcity into a higher price for the next buyer. It is supply and demand written as one equation.
questions.explainWrong: There is no repeat-buyer surcharge. Each swap reduces the SOL reserve, and x · y = k converts that reduction straight into a higher quote.

questions.prompt: Which statement about price impact is TRUE?
options: Price impact only matters for trades under $10
All pools produce identical price impact for the same trade size
Deep pools magnify price impact
Price impact shrinks as pool reserves grow, but grows non-linearly as your trade size approaches the full reserve
questions.explainRight: Price impact scales with order size relative to reserves. Deeper reserves shrink it; a trade that approaches the reserve size blows it up faster than linearly.
questions.explainWrong: It is never uniform across pools, and it is not limited to tiny trades. Impact is a ratio, so it grows worse-than-linearly as your order approaches the pool's reserves.

questions.prompt: You swap the same 50 USDC in two pools: Pool A has $4,000 TVL and Pool B has $400,000 TVL. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Pool B returns noticeably more SOL for the same 50 USDC
Both pools return identical SOL because the trade size is the same
Pool A returns more SOL because it needs the volume
Deep pools reject trades under $100
questions.explainRight: In the $4,000 pool your $50 is a visible share of the vault, so the curve pushes the price hard against you. In the $400,000 pool it is noise. Same input, meaningfully different output.
questions.explainWrong: Identical order size does not mean identical fill. The shallow pool treats your $50 as a large order and hands back less SOL for it.
